sections.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones
sections.heading: C — Occupant protection, steering, braking and seeing around the vehicle
sections.markdown:
## C — Occupant protection, steering, braking and seeing around the vehicle

FACT_ID: sec04-F01 | anchor: A52
Wearing a seat belt correctly is the single most effective way to protect yourself and sharply cuts your risk of a fatal injury in a crash. [A52]
Source: [A52 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F02 | anchor: A52
The shoulder belt goes snugly across the middle of the chest and shoulder, never behind your back, under your arm, or across the neck or face, and the lap belt holds the hips snugly below the stomach. [A52]
Source: [A52 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F03 | anchor: A52
Under RCW 46.61.687 and RCW 46.61.688, all occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint, and driving or riding without one is illegal. [A52]
Why it matters: the rule covers every seat, not only the driver and front passenger.
Source: [A52 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F04 | anchor: A53
Check that the belt is not twisted, the lap portion sits on the upper thighs and the cross strap falls over mid-shoulder, with knees bending at the seat edge, feet on the floor and headrest in line with your ears. [A53]
Source: [A53 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec04-F05 | anchor: A53
Child restraints must meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and be installed following both the vehicle and the seat maker's instructions, and a certified child passenger safety technician can check the installation. [A53]
Source: [A53 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec04-F06 | anchor: A53
Keep a child in each restraint stage as long as that seat allows, and a child from birth until age 2 must use a car seat that faces the rear. [A53]
Source: [A53 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec04-F07 | anchor: A54
Children aged 2 to 4 must ride in a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward. [A54]
Source: [A54 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec04-F08 | anchor: A54
Children aged 4 and older stay in a car or booster seat until the vehicle's lap and shoulder belts fit properly, usually between ages 8 and 12, and the booster stage covers kids from 4 years old up to a height of 4 feet 9 inches. [A54]
Why it matters: a common error is moving a child to the seat belt by age alone instead of by belt fit and height.
Source: [A54 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec04-F09 | anchor: A54
Anyone taller than 4 feet 9 inches who is old enough for a seat belt must wear a properly fitting belt. [A54]
Source: [A54 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec04-F10 | anchor: A54
Airbags work together with seat belts, so an unbelted occupant risks serious injury or death when an airbag deploys, and children under 13 should never ride in the front seat. [A54]
Source: [A54 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec04-F11 | anchor: A55
For the best control, hold the outside of the wheel on its top half, picturing the wheel as a clock face with hands at about 9:00 and 3:00. [A55]
Source: [A55 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec04-F12 | anchor: A56
In hand-to-hand (pull/push) steering your hands sit at 9 and 3 or 10 and 2, each stays on its own side, one hand pulls while the other slides, and the hands never cross. [A56]
Why it matters: because the arms never cross, this method keeps them out of the airbag's path.
Source: [A56 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec04-F13 | anchor: A57
Hand-over-hand steering, starting from 9 and 3 or 10 and 2, is for low-speed turns, limited visibility, intersections, parking and skid recovery: reach one arm across the other, pull, release the lower hand, and straighten the wheel as the turn ends. [A57]
Source: [A57 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec04-F14 | anchor: A58
Use one-hand steering when backing up or when you must reach for controls such as wipers, flashers or lights, and the 12 o'clock hand position is recommended only for backing while you turn your body to look behind. [A58]
Source: [A58 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec04-F15 | anchor: A58
The guide names four braking levels, light, medium, firm and emergency, and judging the right pressure is a skill that grows with practice in your vehicle. [A58]
Source: [A58 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec04-F16 | anchor: A59
Aim to need only light and medium braking, brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap, and avoid needless hard stops that could surprise drivers behind you. [A59]
Source: [A59 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec04-F17 | anchor: A59
An antilock brake system lets you keep steering during an emergency stop but does not shorten your stopping distance, and you may feel the car shake when it engages. [A59]
Why it matters: the most common ABS misconception is that it makes the car stop sooner.
Source: [A59 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec04-F18 | anchor: A59
Practice firm or emergency braking in a large open paved area to feel the ABS stop the wheels from locking. [A59]
Source: [A59 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec04-F19 | anchor: A59
Smooth acceleration follows the same cup-of-water idea, ranging from simply easing off the brake in stop-and-go traffic to speeding up quickly to avoid a hazard. [A59]
Source: [A59 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec04-F20 | anchor: A60
Keeping weight evenly spread across all tires keeps the vehicle stable, helped by regular maintenance, correct tire pressure and alignment checks. [A60]
Source: [A60 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec04-F21 | anchor: A60
Pitch is the forward and backward weight shift: accelerating loads the rear of the vehicle, while a sudden stop loads the front. [A60]
Source: [A60 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec04-F22 | anchor: A61
Roll is the side-to-side weight shift, and in a left turn centrifugal force pushes the weight onto the outside, or right side, of the vehicle. [A61]
Source: [A61 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec04-F23 | anchor: A62
Yaw is the zig-zag that happens when you steer sharply from side to side, because the front wheels follow the steering while the rear may slide out of line. [A62]
Source: [A62 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec04-F24 | anchor: A62
Vehicle reference points such as the left headlight, center of the hood, side mirrors and rear bumper help you judge distance when parking, turning, backing and stopping. [A62]
Source: [A62 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec04-F25 | anchor: A62
When the stop line appears under your side mirror at an intersection, your front end is roughly 3 to 6 inches from that line. [A62]
Source: [A62 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec04-F26 | anchor: A63
When the center of your hood lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly 3 to 6 inches from the edge of the lane. [A63]
Source: [A63 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec04-F27 | anchor: A63
Blind zones are areas you cannot see from the driver's seat that can fully hide a car, motorcyclist or bicyclist, and you are responsible for knowing what is in them. [A63]
Source: [A63 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec04-F28 | anchor: A63
Shrink blind zones by setting the rearview mirror to see out the back window without stretching and setting the side mirrors by the traditional or enhanced method, then still turn your head with the wheel held straight to check. [A63]
Why it matters: blind-zone alerts help, but the guide wants an eye check every time.
Source: [A63 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec04-F29 | anchor: A64
A regular scan covers the road ahead, the rearview mirror, both side mirrors and over both shoulders. [A64]
Source: [A64 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec04-F30 | anchor: A64
Stay out of other drivers' blind zones by adjusting your speed, and take extra care around buses, motor homes and commercial vehicles, whose large blind zones are called no zones. [A64]
Source: [A64 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec04-F31 | anchor: A64
If you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors, its driver cannot see you. [A64]
Source: [A64 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec04-F32 | anchor: A65
Recheck and adjust your mirrors every time you get behind the wheel, and keep checking them for changes while you drive. [A65]
Source: [A65 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec04-F33 | anchor: A66
A good pre-drive routine checks outside the vehicle for tire debris, glass, leaks and obstacles such as children or pets, checks inside for warning lights, clear windows and secured items, confirms mirrors, seat, wheel, belt and a silenced phone, and checks that you feel healthy, focused and calm. [A66]
Source: [A66 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0066]

Glossary: pitch — forward and backward weight shift [A60]. Roll — side-to-side weight shift [A61]. Yaw — the rear sliding out of line during sharp steering [A62]. No zone — a large vehicle's big blind zone [A64]. ABS — antilock brake system [A59].
Memory aid: pitch, roll and yaw match nodding, tilting and wagging your hand on a table, as the guide demonstrates [A60].
